name: a tree with no pointers
hook: A heap is a tree with no pointers. Just an array and three lines of arithmetic.
hook_slide: A heap is a tree with *no pointers*.
hook_sub: Just an array and three lines of arithmetic.
caption: A heap is always a complete binary tree: every level full except possibly the last, and the last filled left to right with no gaps.
Number the nodes in reading order and write them into an array. A node at index i has its children at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, and its parent at (i − 1) // 2. No pointer is ever stored.
In [1, 3, 2, 7, 4, 5, 8], index {i}'s children are indices {l} and {r} (values {lv} and {rv}), and index {c}'s parent is index {pc}.
It only works because there are no gaps. And it saves real memory: a pointer-based tree of {n} nodes spends {pointer_bytes} bytes on child references alone.
Did you know the heap in your standard library is just a list? 👇
cta: Next: sift up and sift down, the two moves that keep it a heap.

p: Every level is entirely full except possibly the last, and the last is filled strictly left to right.
Number the nodes in reading order, write them into a flat array, and the whole tree is still there.
A node's parent and children are found by pure index arithmetic. Not a single pointer is stored.
Every parent is no bigger than its children: a min-heap, stored flat.
With no gaps, the level sizes are exact powers of two. That counting is what collapses the algebra to `2i + 1` and `2i + 2`.
A node missing in the middle of a level would break the arithmetic. Completeness is not cosmetic: it lets the array *be* the tree.
Two child references are {ref_bytes} bytes on a 64-bit machine. For an int-sized payload, the pointers can outweigh the data.
